controls_moving_around.title: Controls: Moving Around
controls_moving_around.description:
Arrows or WASD move. Z or Enter confirms and talks, X or Escape cancels. Hold Shift to run.

Running spends AP, the same meter battle skills use. Walk or stand still to refill it.

Z acts on whatever you face. Z on a companion opens their Empathize sheet.

C kicks. Kicks break crates, force doors and shove objects. If nothing makes a sound, it can't be kicked. Locked doors take several kicks.

controls_menu_hotkeys.title: Controls: Menu Hotkeys
controls_menu_hotkeys.description:
Tab opens the menu. Each screen also has a letter, pressed on the map:

- I inventory, C character, R equipment, P skills, J quests
- M minimap, B build, V vehicles, F factions, H holdings
- K cooking, L this book, N training, Y bestiary, U biologics
- O options, G sandbox (tester builds)

Inside the menu: 1 Thinker, 2 multiplayer, 3 Hypernet. On the map, 1 to 9 fire the quick bar.

WASD, Z, X, Q, E and T are reserved. F9 quicksave, F10 quickload, F11 fullscreen.

controls_mouse.title: Controls: Mouse
controls_mouse.description:
The mouse does not move your character.

- drag pans the camera, it snaps back when you walk
- wheel zooms, world map only
- hover shows an event's label, Alt labels them all

In battle: left click an enemy to hit it with the selected command, right click cycles commands, wheel scrolls, 1 to 5 fire.

Menus are clickable throughout.

controls_controller.title: Controls: Controller
controls_controller.description:
A controller works everywhere, menus, star map and 3D minigames included.

- left stick moves and navigates, right stick pans
- R3 labels every event on screen
- L2 / R2 zoom the world map, the right stick scrolls long overlays
- L1 / R1 cycle tabs, change character, step the quick bar

One thing still needs a mouse: opening a search field.

controls_remapping.title: Controls: Remapping
controls_remapping.description:
Options, Commands page. Keyboard and gamepad remap separately, and every default command can be rebound.

The ones added here: Zoom In (Q, LB), Zoom Out (E, RB), Kick (C, RT), Run (Shift, LT).

Bindings are kept with your settings.

what_is_on_the_screen.title: What Is On The Screen
what_is_on_the_screen.description:
The party HUD sits top left, on the map and in battle: name, level, HP, AP orb, MP. The acting member is lit.

Chips run beside each card. Hunger, sleep, hygiene, cravings and illness on the map; stat changes, class resources and states in battle. They colour past the warning line and again past the critical one.

While riding, the vehicle takes a row above the crew, fuel where magic would be.

The quick bar sits bottom centre: items on the map, skills in battle.

Notifications are parchment cards. Transient ones fade; standing ones stay while they are true.

The HUD can be switched off in Options, Video.

searching_inside_menus.title: Searching Inside Menus
searching_inside_menus.description:
Every long list has a search bar, this book included. It starts as a magnifier at the top of the page.

- while typing, menu hotkeys are off
- Escape clears the field, Escape again leaves it

The main menu search covers several screens at once: carried items, companions' gear, skills, recipes you can make now, bestiary creatures.

saving,_autosave_and_quicksaves.title: Saving, Autosave and Quicksaves
saving,_autosave_and_quicksaves.description:
The game autosaves on map change, at most once every few minutes, into an ordinary slot.

F9 quicksaves, F10 quickloads, over three rotating slots that any playthrough may overwrite.

Deleting a permadeath save leaves its diary behind.

worlds_and_savegames.title: Worlds and Savegames
worlds_and_savegames.description:
A world is a folder, and several can sit side by side. Make them from the Worlds screen. Until one exists, Explore, Reconnect, Story Mode and Sandbox stay greyed out.

A world is generated in full before it is played: a century of history, people, homes, jobs, shop rotas, the dungeon, politics, factions, epidemics.

Every playthrough in that world walks into the same place, already changed by the ones before it. The clock only moves forward, so a loaded save resumes from the latest date reached there.

Other playthroughs appear in person, standing where they were last saved.

options.title: Options
options.description:
Options is split into tabs:

- Video: resolution, fullscreen, pixel perfect scaling, retro shader, UI scaling, party HUD
- Audio: volumes, battle music picker
- Gameplay: party formation, auto idle explorer, world map hints
- Commands: keyboard and gamepad remapping
- Experimental: includes a local language model that writes NPC dialogue

Fullscreen is on the first time the game runs, then keeps your setting.

mods_and_updates.title: Mods and Updates
mods_and_updates.description:
Mods go in the mods folder next to the executable. A mod can replace data, add pictures or add content. Desktop build only.

In the Mod Manager, Enter toggles a mod and arrows change the load order. The bottom of the list wins.

Updates on the title screen downloads only the files that changed. Replaced files are backed up, and the game must be restarted. Pick the stable or unstable channel, or restore any earlier build.

the_party.title: The Party
the_party.description:
Three members. The first is the leader: the one you steer, whose needs drain fastest and who NPCs talk to.

A fourth companion can walk along without being a member. It never fights and cannot be hurt.

Each member has their own needs, opinions, reputation, specializations and relationships with the other two.

Set formation in Options. Close keeps everyone behind the leader; Loose lets them wander and regroup off screen. Loose members look after themselves when a need runs low, paying from the party's money.

Run for a moment to call everyone back. Face a companion and confirm to open their Empathize sheet.

making_your_characters.title: Making Your Characters
making_your_characters.description:
Characters are made one at a time, three ways:

- Quick: look, class, traits, gear
- Dossiers: pre-made characters, some reusable in any world, the rest spent once used. A dossier may bring a vehicle, a hometown and alternate skins
- Detailed: the whole sheet, down to ideology, morality, orientation and backstory

Starting gear is picked by price, not power: the cheapest weapon of each type, on a fixed budget per class. Trait gear is granted on top.

classes.title: Classes
classes.description:
A class sets starting stats, the schools you learn fastest and a favoured element.

Each class has a primary and a secondary category. Primary skills progress fastest and cost least, secondary ones progress faster at normal price. Skills from other schools need a known skill in that school first and cost much more.

Training lists your class curriculum, but other skills can still be learned.

Any class can equip any weapon. Weapon skill is trained separately.

Creature classes are a separate set: Feral, Mimic, Monster, Mana Cyborg, Ghost, Zombie, Mutant, Drone. A character with one of them counts as an animal.

traits.title: Traits
traits.description:
Traits are bought at creation from a pool of points. Positive traits cost, negative traits pay back, so drawbacks fund virtues.

They change base stats and grant skills, items and gear, and they are read during play: NPC first impressions, how much anyone minds your condition, which specializations start ahead, what companions do with their free time.

Traits are permanent.

attributes.title: Attributes
attributes.description:
Six attributes:

- STR: carrying capacity, physical damage
- CON: damage absorbed, how long a choke is held
- DEX: speed, precision, evasion, escaping holds
- INT: learning, mathematical magic
- WIS: judgement, resistance, intuitive magic
- PSI: luck. Enemy reactions, loot rolls, hidden rolls in your favour

The battle HUD shows the modifier as a multiplier (STR 1.4x).

playing_a_creature.title: Playing A Creature
playing_a_creature.description:
A party member can be a creature, built from one archetype or two crossed.

The archetype sets the body: that species' parts, reach, hands and weak points.

A creature class is non sentient: no conversation, politics, savings or property. A civilised class is a person shaped like an animal, and is treated as a person.

Anatomy affects play. It decides how many weapons can be held, whether you can be choked, and what a pregnancy produces.

portraits_and_3d_models.title: Portraits and 3D Models
portraits_and_3d_models.description:
Each character is drawn one of three ways, chosen at creation and never mixed:

- bust: hand drawn portrait
- model: procedural 3D body. Each limb can take the matching part of any registered creature, with sliders for height, build, ears, nose and skin
- sprite: used by monsters, recruited enemies and summons, shown as the 3D model of their species

The status screen, the dialogue busts and the Empathize panel all use it.

recruiting_people.title: Recruiting People
recruiting_people.description:
Three ways into the party: talk a monster round in battle, ask a townsperson through Empathize once they think well enough of whoever is asking, or adopt a creature and train it up.

A recruited townsperson leaves the map for good. Their profile, personality, traits, skills, wealth, history and standing all move into the party actor.

The party holds three, so someone must leave for someone to join. Retired members go back to the dossier board.

pets,_followers_and_children.title: Pets, Followers and Children
pets,_followers_and_children.description:
A fourth companion follows the party without being a member. It never fights, cannot die and cannot be targeted.

A follower is a creature recruited from a monster that talks, a pet one from a monster that does not, a child the result of a pregnancy.

Only one walks with you at a time; the Followers page swaps and releases them.

Pets and followers can be trained into party members, at classes the species roster allows. Training is measured in world clock minutes, Animal Training or Leadership shortens it, and only the companion currently walking with you makes progress. Children and summons are never trained.

reproduction_and_pregnancy.title: Reproduction and Pregnancy
reproduction_and_pregnancy.description:
Every body has a reproductive type, set by its species:

- Testicles: fertility depends on hormones and condition
- Uterus: a monthly cycle with a few fertile days
- Oviparous: lays a clutch of eggs
- Plant: makes seeds that pile up until planted
- Mitosis: the body divides into a copy

A pregnancy lasts as long as the species needs. Biologics shows its progress, symptoms arrive as states, and the heart rate climbs.

Newborns appear in Followers as children with the parent's face. Mitosis makes a copy of the parent.

death,_gravestones_and_permadeath.title: Death, Gravestones and Permadeath
death,_gravestones_and_permadeath.description:
Falling in battle is not automatic death. Health protection and danger warnings let you break off, and fleeing always works.

A dead character leaves a gravestone where they fell. It stays on the map and is where restoration is performed.

Under permadeath the character is gone for good and their quicksaves with them. A wiped party ends that party only; the next starts in the same changed world.

Lost limbs are not death and healing does not put them back.

what_your_companions_say.title: What Your Companions Say
what_your_companions_say.description:
Two or more companions chat about what is going on: a recent purchase, low health, a need running low, something from the diary, the biome, the road, money, the leader, the plan.

Personality shapes each line, so the same topic plays out differently depending on who is in the party.

They also talk while driving and on trains, coaches and taxis. A party of one talks to itself.

the_auto_explorer.title: The Auto Explorer
the_auto_explorer.description: An Options toggle plays the game for you while you are idle. The party explores, crosses the map and looks after its needs the way a loose companion does, paying the same costs you would, and gives control back as soon as you press any key.

levels_and_experience.title: Levels and Experience
levels_and_experience.description:
Experience comes from winning fights, and a level raises the six attributes and the HP and MP pools.

Levels are a small part of power. Skills learned, specializations trained, gear carried and the condition of the body all matter more.

knowledge_points.title: Knowledge Points
knowledge_points.description:
Knowledge points (KP) buy skills and are shared by the whole party. You earn them from fights, quests, adventures, dreams and Raman scans.

Stronger skills cost more. Esoteric and Forbidden skills cost far more.

Skills from your primary school are cheapest, secondary ones cost the normal price, other schools cost the most.

the_atlas_of_circles.title: The Atlas of Circles
the_atlas_of_circles.description:
Skills are laid out as a sphere grid. Each school is a circle: rings run from its weakest skills outward to its strongest, with upgrade branches on the rim.

You can buy a skill only if it is next to one you know. The inner ring of every school is always open.

Forbidden skills sit alone in the centre. They open only once you know the whole school.

One school at a time: use the pager or walk off the rim. Wheel and Shift zoom, drag pans.

training_and_progression.title: Training and Progression
training_and_progression.description: Each member trains one skill at a time. Winning battles and using skills of the same category both advance it. Primary categories train fastest, secondary ones faster than the rest.

specializations.title: Specializations
specializations.description:
Hundreds of specializations, from Wrestling to Accounting to Beekeeping. Each uses one attribute and has five tiers, Untrained to Master.

Your level is the highest of: trained through play, granted by class, granted by a trait.

They train by doing. Cooking raises Cooking, selling raises Haggling. The leader gains the most, others present gain less.

They affect forging quality, lockpicking, holds, what merchants accept and which recipes you can read.

class_passives.title: Class Passives
class_passives.description:
Every class has signature passives. They need no slot and no activation. Some work in combat, some only outside it.

They are listed on the status sheet under Passives.

the_nine_skill_slots.title: The Nine Skill Slots
the_nine_skill_slots.description:
Each character takes nine skills into a fight. The skill menu is tabbed by role, and the nine you pick fill the battle quick bar.

You never forget a skill, and changing the nine between fights is free.

fusing_spells.title: Fusing Spells
fusing_spells.description:
From the Magic page, two abilities can be forged into one. The dominant slot takes a spell you know and sets damage, scope, hit type and icon. The recessive slot takes a spell or a skill, and a skill makes the result a skill.

The fusion costs the sum of its parts in MP and AP, and the sum of their teaching prices in KP. The components are forgotten on fusing, and the fusion can be split back into them at any time.

grimoires_and_skill_books.title: Grimoires and Skill Books
grimoires_and_skill_books.description:
A grimoire offers five random spells and one reader picks one. The offers are fixed when the book is opened; switching reader does not change them.

You can only take a spell you don't know and can afford with your max MP. Higher PSI makes Forbidden spells more likely.

There are school grimoires, category skill books, and the Forbidden Grimoire, which offers only Forbidden spells.

expression_seeds.title: Expression Seeds
expression_seeds.description:
An expression seed is used on one character and unlocks their Expression. Each character needs a seed of their own.

Expression is opened from the skills benches, picking any party member who has it.

A power can be bound by limitations: never on a chosen day, only against one kind of creature, only by night, only at a price in blood or gold. The more a power is bound, the less it costs, and the further it can reach beyond the character's stats.

equipment_hands_and_slots.title: Equipment: Hands and Slots
equipment_hands_and_slots.description:
Weapon slots come from anatomy: every body part that can hold a weapon is a slot. Hands take a weapon or a shield, so two shields work as well as two swords.

- a two handed weapon needs two free hands
- a body with no hands holds its weapon in the mouth. Samurai get a mouth slot as well as their hands
- eight slots at most
- with more than two weapons, stats are averaged and two random weapons swing each turn
- losing a limb removes its slot and drops what it held

weapon_proficiency.title: Weapon Proficiency
weapon_proficiency.description:
Any class can equip any weapon type. Skill with each weapon type is its own specialization. It starts at Intermediate for your class's traditional weapons and Untrained for the rest.

Higher tiers make the weapon stronger. Untrained wielders get much less out of it.

Winning a battle trains every equipped weapon type.

what_a_weapon_scales_on.title: What a Weapon Scales On
what_a_weapon_scales_on.description: A weapon does not always scale on STR. Its attack skill sets the attribute it reads, and the equip screen names it when the slot is selected. With no attack skill it reads STR; otherwise DEX, INT, WIS, CON, PSI, or a mix of two.

armour_and_derived_stats.title: Armour and Derived Stats
armour_and_derived_stats.description:
Equipment feeds four out of combat stats besides defence. Clothes give Substance and Stealth, robes Arcane, light armour Stealth, heavy armour Intimidation.

Weapons feed them too: daggers and bows Stealth, swords, heavy weapons, axes and claws Intimidation, staves Arcane, whips, projectiles and guns Substance.

They decide how people answer you, what a guard assumes, which approaches are open.

modifiers_on_gear.title: Modifiers on Gear
modifiers_on_gear.description:
A weapon or armour piece can have one modifier, which changes its stats, price and traits. Sharp raises STR and price on weapons, Refined raises CON, WIS and price on anything, Poisoned adds poison to a weapon, Worn lowers CON, WIS and price on armour.

The modifier stays with the item.

weight_and_encumbrance.title: Weight and Encumbrance
weight_and_encumbrance.description: Every item has a weight and the party has a carry capacity. Going over it raises a standing notification that stays up until you are back under.

the_backpack.title: The Backpack
the_backpack.description:
The backpack is tabbed by category, with the weight readout, the detail card and the favourites bar.

Nine favourite slots hold usable items and share the quick bar with battle skills. On the map, 1 to 9 use that slot; in the backpack, the same keys assign the inspected item. Items can be dragged onto slots, right click clears one.

Only usable items can be favourited. Weapons and armour are equipped instead.

artifacts.title: Artifacts
artifacts.description:
Artifacts are procedurally generated items, weapons and armour, each named and unique.

The Artifact Analyzer on the Hypernet reads what an unfamiliar one does.

containers_and_storage.title: Containers and Storage
containers_and_storage.description:
Chests, cupboards, crates and sacks store items and can be emptied or filled at will.

The party's own storage travels with it: the extradimensional container, and the holds of the camper and the car.

loot_and_rarity.title: Loot and Rarity
loot_and_rarity.description:
Random loot is scaled against the party's median level, not the leader's.

Items print in their rarity colour everywhere: reward popup, backpack, shop counter.

Item descriptions are combinatorial and resolved from the world seed, so the same sword reads the same way all through one world and differently in the next.

the_five_needs.title: The Five Needs
the_five_needs.description:
Everyone, your party included, has five needs: Hunger, Sleep, Hygiene, Company and Fun.

They drop as time passes, and time passes as you walk, faster on the world map. The leader's drop fastest, and running drains them all faster.

They show as chips beside each party card and change colour when low and when empty.

An empty Hunger drains HP, an empty Sleep drains MP, and the others cost you socially and mentally.

Augments can slow, stop or reverse a need.

hunger_and_nutrition.title: Hunger and Nutrition
hunger_and_nutrition.description:
Food has calories, fat and protein. A meal's value comes from what is in it, not its price.

You can eat past full, but overeating gives the Overfed state and burns food faster.

Cold and heat both make you hungry faster.

With Hunger empty you keep losing HP until you eat.

sleep,_rest_and_time_awake.title: Sleep, Rest and Time Awake
sleep,_rest_and_time_awake.description:
Two separate things are tracked.

The Sleep meter is how tired you feel. Coffee or sitting down refills it, and when empty it drains MP.

Time awake counts since your last real sleep, and only a night's rest resets it. The longer you stay awake, the worse your dreams get and the more the party's mind suffers.

Beds, campfires, tents and world map camps open the rest menu. Waiting and the T hotkey only move the clock. Cryogenic sleep lets you pick a year to wake in while the world moves on.

hygiene,_and_what_it_costs_you.title: Hygiene, and What It Costs You
hygiene,_and_what_it_costs_you.description:
Refill Hygiene at a washroom, shower, sink or fountain. Loose companions go and find one when they need it.

People notice how you smell, and you notice them. Low hygiene lowers what others think of you.

Traits decide how much it matters. Feral ignores it, Ascetic barely notices, Street Urchin, Cave Dweller, Survivalist, Farmer and Veteran mind little. Proud, Wealthy, Beautiful, Perfectionist, Noble, Hypochondriac and Germaphobe mind a lot.

It matters even more when courting.

company.title: Company
company.description:
Company drains like any other need and is refilled by talking, to townspeople or between two of your own.

A loose member starved of company walks up to someone and starts a conversation unprompted. That conversation moves what the other person thinks of them, and hygiene counts in it.

Gaining standing with someone feeds the social meter of whoever gained it.

fun.title: Fun
fun.description:
Fun is refilled by playing: arcade cabinets, pianos, pool tables, card games, and jokes that land in conversation. A joke that lands also raises the listener's Fun for the rest of the day.

A party with Fun on the floor complains about it in banter.

cravings_and_withdrawal.title: Cravings and Withdrawal
cravings_and_withdrawal.description:
Five traits are addictions: alcohol, caffeine, nicotine, narcotics and gambling. Only a member with one has a craving meter.

The craving climbs while unfed and drops when you feed it. A full meter means withdrawal, and one dose is not enough to end it.

Cravings climb slower while asleep.

limbs_and_organs.title: Limbs and Organs
limbs_and_organs.description:
Every character and monster has individual limbs and organs, each with its own health.

Damage spreads across parts. A part at 0 is destroyed and changes what the body can do: a lost hand loses its weapon slot, a body with no hands holds a weapon in its mouth, damaged legs cost movement and evasion. Damaged or destroyed parts can't grapple or be grappled.

Vital organs can only be hit by aiming at them, and a blow to one is only fatal once its owner is badly hurt.

Parts never heal on their own. Treat them at a clinic, restore them with magic, or replace them with a prosthetic. In Blood and Oil a slashing or piercing blow can cut a part off, augment included.

The status sheet's Anatomy section shows the body part by part.

biologics.title: Biologics
biologics.description:
Biologics is the deep readout: vital signs, hormones, blood chemistry, brain regions and their activity, blood type, reproductive cycle, and every condition acting on the body.

Heart rate reacts to what is happening to you, hormones to sleep, injury and pregnancy. Blood type is set once and never changes.

The Ley Vein system links it to limb damage: blockages show up here when the body has been hurt.

diseases.title: Diseases
diseases.description:
Hundreds of diseases exist. Each spreads in its own ways (airborne, saliva, bite, contact, sexual and others), changes stats while you have it, and often shows symptoms only after a while. That delay is the window period.

Diseases can pass between party members and between you and anyone you talk to through Empathize. Sexual diseases don't spread by proximity.

Every NPC has a medical history, shown on the Health tab of their panel.

Diagnose checks the whole party and names every illness, even ones still in the window period.

epidemics.title: Epidemics
epidemics.description:
Epidemics spread across the continent whether you watch or not. They travel between towns, and towns fight back the longer they are infected.

An outbreak is a real disease that can kill. A hysteria is not: dancing fever, panics, phantom gassers. You catch a hysteria by seeing it and spread it by talking about it.

Every world starts with three running: one hysteria, one ordinary outbreak, one rare and deadly.

Anyone in an infected town is exposed, you included. Outbreaks affect mood, jobs, shops, needs, gossip and the news. Track them in the Eurodemics app.

clinics,_prosthetics_and_field_surgery.title: Clinics, Prosthetics and Field Surgery
clinics,_prosthetics_and_field_surgery.description:
A clinic can install, remove or replace a body part, or fit an implant. Bigger parts cost more to install. Vital parts can't be removed.

Field surgery works on the road and is free: pick a patient and a surgeon. You can only fit parts you carry, and you can remove an augment but not install one.

Every operation can fail, and the odds are shown first. A better Surgery specialization helps, a roof helps, bad weather and the open air hurt, and operating on yourself is harder.

A failure wounds the patient elsewhere. Vital organs are only at risk in Blood and Oil.

augments.title: Augments
augments.description:
The Augments register has two lists. Fitted is every augment the party wears, with its wearer and socket. Catalogue is everything that exists, readable before paying to have it grafted.

The dossier gives the cost, the bonus, the skill it teaches, and every socket that accepts it, creature sockets included.

Augments are also how the needs system is bent: the right hardware slows a meter, stops it, or reverses it.

weather,_temperature_and_the_body.title: Weather, Temperature and the Body
weather,_temperature_and_the_body.description:
Temperature is shown on the travel card and affects the body. Cold and heat both make hunger drop faster.

Bad weather makes field surgery riskier, and changes what people do and where they go.

how_a_fight_starts.title: How a Fight Starts
how_a_fight_starts.description:
There are no random encounters. Every monster stands on the map with its level over its head, and you fight it by walking into it.

Turns are individual: each battler acts when its own turn comes up, in agility order, and your action resolves as soon as you choose it.

Enemies keep their damage between fights. A wounded monster you ran from is still wounded when you come back, and corpses stay on the map.

Fleeing always works.

the_battle_commands.title: The Battle Commands
the_battle_commands.description:
The command menu holds Attack, Guard, Skills, Magic, Item, Escape, Reload when a firearm is empty, and four of its own:

- Check: opens the enemy's body, limb by limb, with the chance of hitting each
- Target: aims your next blow at one part
- Wrestle: takes hold of the enemy
- Talk: another way to end a fight

Wrestle and Talk are commands, not skills. They take no loadout slot, cannot be forgotten, and come from the body rather than the class.

Mouse: left click an enemy to run the selected command on it, right click cycles, wheel scrolls, 1 to 5 fire.

mp_and_ap.title: MP and AP
mp_and_ap.description:
Two resources. MP is magic: spells cost it, it refills slowly, and most rites and summons are kept up with it.

AP is stamina, used by battle skills and by running on the map. Walking refills it slowly, standing still faster.

Spells are written in CamelCase and cost MP. Skills are written in plain words and cost AP.

hitting_what_you_aim_at.title: Hitting What You Aim At
hitting_what_you_aim_at.description:
Monsters have limbs and organs just like the party. Check lists every part with its condition and your chance to hit it, and Target aims your next blow at one. Bigger parts are easier to hit, and your weapon and stats matter.

Destroying a limb removes what it does: a broken leg slows, a ruined wing stops flight, no hands means no weapon. Vital organs can only be hit by targeting them.

Part damage lasts the whole fight, and a finishing blow can cut the part off.

wrestling.title: Wrestling
wrestling.description:
Wrestle is open to any body with one limb whole enough to grip. It costs nothing and is never learned.

It replaces the command menu with the grapple plan: which of your limbs takes the hold, which of theirs it is taken on, and which hold. Each row shows the odds. A part at 0, damaged or severed can neither grab nor be grabbed, on either side.

- Grapple, STR against DEX: takes hold. Everything else needs one first
- Strike, STR against DEX: needs no hold, can concuss on the head
- Joint lock, DEX against STR: pins, often breaks the guard
- Wrench, STR against CON: heavy damage, can cause bleeding
- Slam, CON against DEX: guard broken, winded, chance to stun
- Choke, CON against CON, head only: guard broken, vitals exposed
- Rip, STR against CON: low odds, enormous damage, can tear the limb off

Everything scales with the Wrestling specialization. Any trained martial art adds its own finishers without them being learned as skills.

talking_to_monsters.title: Talking to Monsters
talking_to_monsters.description:
Monsters that can understand you can be talked to. Talk opens a panel showing the odds of each option.

Each enemy has a mood towards you. Its species shapes it, hurting it lowers it, and your PSI against its own helps.

- Chat builds rapport
- Surrender asks it to leave the fight
- Join the party needs a free slot and a friendly enemy
- Follow you, or be adopted as a pet, needs a friendly enemy
- Insult always works and makes it angrier
- Throw a stone, or pet it

Some creatures, petrodemons above all, refuse every approach.

One talked into joining becomes a party member. A pet or follower can be trained into a member later.

enemy_levels_and_where_they_live.title: Enemy Levels and Where They Live
enemy_levels_and_where_they_live.description:
The Enemy Spawn option sets how enemy levels are chosen.

- Balanced: enemies are a bit above your party's level, with the odd boss above that
- Distance from spawn (default): enemies get stronger the farther you are from where you started
- Chaos: any level, rerolled every time you enter a map

Each square has creatures that fit its biome. No creature is exclusive to a country; nations only change how common each one is.

The calendar matters too: enemies get stronger as the years go by.

how_monsters_behave.title: How Monsters Behave
how_monsters_behave.description:
Each roaming monster has a movement personality that sets what it does while idle, how it notices you (sight range, facing cone, line of sight) and what it does once it has.

Fixed, Random, Approach, Fleeing, Skittish, Grazer, Sentry, Guard, Patrol, Territorial, Ambusher, Lurker, Mimic, Swooper, Stalker, Hunter, Charger, Pack, Erratic, Drifter, Orbiter, Scavenger, Coward.

A Grazer never notices you. A Sentry has a cone and can be walked around. An Ambusher is not where it appears to be. A Pack does not fight alone.

danger_warnings_and_surviving_a_blow.title: Danger Warnings and Surviving a Blow
danger_warnings_and_surviving_a_blow.description:
Before a fight the party's median level is compared with the enemy, and a warning appears when it is out of range. Enemy levels are drawn over their heads on the map.

Inside a fight each character has one health protection charge: the first blow that would kill them leaves them at 1 HP. It comes back next battle. Blood and Oil removes it.

difficulty_and_combat_modes.title: Difficulty and Combat Modes
difficulty_and_combat_modes.description:
Several settings change what combat is, most chosen at character creation.

- Peaceful: monsters act only once hurt, per enemy. An unprovoked one skips its turn, roaming monsters wander instead of chasing, and a wipe respawns you with nobody dead
- Ordinary: death leaves a gravestone and the run continues
- Hardcore and Blood and Oil: death is a game over and the character is removed. Blood and Oil also drops the health protection charge and lets a slashing blow take a part off the body
- Card combat: replaces the command menu
- Map battle: fights on the live map

map_battle_mode.title: Map Battle Mode
map_battle_mode.description:
An experimental option that fights every battle on the map you are on, with no separate battle screen.

Everyone fights from where they stand. Nearby monsters can join in, and townspeople nearby may help you if they like the party or are brave.

Move repositions the acting battler; faster battlers move farther. Weapons have reach: melee is adjacent, spears, whips, staves and flails reach farther, bows, guns and thrown weapons farther still, and need line of sight. Water means swimming, which costs more movement.

Turn order: party and enemies by agility, then townspeople, then everything else on the map moves one step.

card_combat.title: Card Combat
card_combat.description:
Another way to fight, chosen at character creation or turned on in the experimental options. A fight already running keeps its mode; the change applies from the next one.

Each member has their own deck, hand and energy, built from their class skills. Playing a card is that member's whole turn.

Energy replaces MP and AP. Cards cost energy based on the skill, and a plain attack is cheapest. You gain energy each turn, and passing gives extra energy and a card.

Cheap cards come up most often, and your opening hand always has something you can play.

summons.title: Summons
summons.description:
A summon is a temporary fourth member. In battle it lasts for that fight only, and leaves when the fight ends or when you stop paying for it.

It can be a creature, a person the party has marked, your pet, a reflection of the summoner, or the ghost of a lost companion.

Its strength matches your party and the enemies on the field. A familiar is weaker than a party member, a titan a bit stronger.

Each kind has an upkeep: HP, MP, AP, euros, soul, oil, or a fixed number of turns. When you can't pay, it leaves, and a summoner who can't pay in blood drops to 1 HP.

The familiar belongs to one character, and their class decides which creature answers. Changing class changes the familiar.

While a summon is out, damage the party deals fills a hyper bar. When full, the summon unleashes its ultimate.

Summons are always computer controlled and don't get the 1 HP protection.

Outside battle the same rites work, and the summon walks with you for as long as you pay MP.

the_arena.title: The Arena
the_arena.description:
The arena offers fights for their own sake, in two forms: a gauntlet, a run of fights in a chosen level bracket, and a biome trial, a run against the fauna of a chosen biome.

The party is rescaled to the bracket, and a random roster can be fielded instead of your own.

Consecutive wins build a streak, with growing rewards of money and items.

bullet_hell_sequences.title: Bullet Hell Sequences
bullet_hell_sequences.description:
Some fights break into a bullet hell sequence: you steer a small craft, dodge the enemy's pattern and shoot back.

Damage taken and dealt there counts in the fight.

Some enemy ultimates must be dodged this way before they land: the more shots you take, the harder the blow. Bullet Time slows the enemy fire. Fights on the map skip the dodge and the blow lands as usual.

spirit_battlers.title: Spirit Battlers
spirit_battlers.description:
Defeated enemies join a spirit roster. One can be fielded in place of an ordinary battler, at a cost that scales with what it was.

The feature has its own switch; with it off, battles are ordinary.

mimicry.title: Mimicry
mimicry.description:
Six mimic skills copy other bodies:

- Partial mimicry: the enemy's face and map sprite, numbers unchanged
- Full mimicry: stats, HP, MP, AP, skills, body and looks
- Mirror: re-executes the enemy's last skill against it
- Copy ally: a companion's name, class, skills, sprite and body
- Random: full mimicry of a creature drawn at random
- Mutation: merges two random archetypes into your own body parts

All six need exactly one enemy on the field. Copying a body copies its limbs, which changes what you can hold and where you can be hurt.

throwing_things.title: Throwing Things
throwing_things.description:
Items, weapons and armour can be thrown a short distance in any direction. Heavy things don't go far but land hard.

A thrown item stays where it lands and anyone can pick it up.

corpses,_rewards_and_cooldowns.title: Corpses, Rewards and Cooldowns
corpses,_rewards_and_cooldowns.description:
After a fight the reward popup names everything at once: items in their rarity colours, money, experience and knowledge, the last scaled by enemy level against the party median.

The dead leave corpses on the map, and enemy events are removed or put behind a cooldown rather than respawning at once.

Every creature met is written into the Bestiary.

elements_how_they_work.title: Elements: How They Work
elements_how_they_work.description:
Nine damage types: Physical, Fire, Ice, Thunder, Water, Petro, Wind, Sacred, Cursed.

Every creature answers each with a rate. Above 100% is a weakness, below is resistance, 0% is immunity, and a negative rate absorbs the element and heals from it.

The battle HUD shows what you have discovered about the enemy in front of you, and the Bestiary keeps it.

States interact: Wet raises lightning damage, Oily raises fire damage, Static absorbs lightning. A class leans toward an element, and a weapon or modifier can have one.

element_physical.title: Element: Physical
element_physical.description:
Edges, points, weight and fists. Most weapons deal it and most armour is built to stop it.

Physical damage severs limbs, breaks guards and lands holds. Heavy armour resists it and feeds Intimidation, light armour trades that for Stealth.

Spirits, oozes and gases resist it.

element_fire.title: Element: Fire
element_fire.description:
Applies Burned, which keeps dealing damage after the blow.

Raised against anything oily, dry or wooden. Resisted by the wet and the cold blooded, absorbed by things that live in fire.

element_ice.title: Element: Ice
element_ice.description:
Applies Cold, and Freeze at strength, which stops a body acting.

Raised against wet targets. Used on a burning target it removes the burn.

element_thunder.title: Element: Thunder
element_thunder.description:
Applies Static, and Paralysis at strength.

Devastating against a wet target. Absorbed by anything already Static, which heals it instead.

Machines and constructs usually resist it.

element_water.title: Element: Water
element_water.description:
Applies Wet, which raises lightning damage, lowers fire damage and is read by several states.

Its own damage is low.

element_petro.title: Element: Petro
element_petro.description:
Oil and what comes out of the ground with it.

Petro belongs to the petrodemons, which cannot be talked to, petted or reasoned with, and which drop barrels rather than coins. Oil works as a currency: it prices the post between worlds, it holds the petrodemon summon on the field, and the market trades it.

Petro damage leaves the target flammable.

element_wind.title: Element: Wind
element_wind.description:
Air, pressure and cutting motion. It unbalances and displaces.

Flying creatures deal it and resist it. It is weakest against rooted or heavy targets.

element_sacred.title: Element: Sacred
element_sacred.description:
Strong against the undead and the cursed. It is the one damage type that heals its target when that target is on the right side of the line.

Sacred workings usually add protection and purging to the damage, and several sit deep in expensive schools.

element_cursed.title: Element: Cursed
element_cursed.description:
Rot, ruin and draining. Dealt by the undead, countered by Sacred.

Cursed spells often cost more than MP, and the strongest are Forbidden, which makes them very expensive to learn.

Strong against the living. It heals the undead.

the_world_map.title: The World Map
the_world_map.description:
The world map is one map of Europe, each tile a whole region. Walking one costs ten minutes of game time, two in a vehicle.

M cycles the display: hidden, corner minimap, fullscreen. In fullscreen, drag to pan, wheel or Q and E to zoom.

Stepping onto a tile offers to keep going or to visit the square, which builds its local map. T switches between the world map and the last local map.

On the world map, loose companions stay within two tiles of the leader, and squares marked "???" are adventures.

procedural_maps.title: Procedural Maps
procedural_maps.description:
Almost every map is generated. A world map square becomes a map when you enter it, and it is the same map every time you return.

The biome sets the terrain and what grows there. Roads, rivers and coastlines line up with the neighbouring squares, and hand made pieces are mixed in.

Walking off the edge takes you to the next square.

biomes.title: Biomes
biomes.description:
The biome of a square sets its tileset, terrain features, fauna, music, weather and forageables.

Some are special variants, rolled rather than fixed: spirit woods, crystal fields. Certain creatures live only there, and a special biome always places at least one of them, whatever the spawn mode or the calendar.

Roofed biomes, cellars, temple interiors, cave dens and dungeons, are entered through a structure entrance instead of walked into.

structures_under_the_map.title: Structures Under the Map
structures_under_the_map.description:
Entrances on procedural maps are walked into, not pressed. What lies behind is rolled from the world seed, the square and the tile, so one stairway always leads to the same place.

- stairs down: any structure. Cellar, dungeon, crypt, catacombs, mine, cistern, warren, oubliette, library, forge, bunker, laboratory, shrine, tunnel, grotto, lava tube, barrow, station, salt works, cave den, temple
- stairs up: things built above ground and since buried
- cave: dens, frozen caves, crystal caves, fungal caves, lava tubes, sea grottoes
- grate: a sewer, only in towns that declare one underneath
- hatch: a Holy Patron Bunker, full of money and rare weapons

The surface limits the options: ice fields hold frozen caves, a graveyard holds catacombs.

houses,_inns_and_shops.title: Houses, Inns and Shops
houses,_inns_and_shops.description:
Doors on generated maps lead to houses, inns, shops and tower blocks. The same door always leads to the same place.

Buildings can have several floors. Shops and inns show their name over the door.

Doors open when you walk into them, unless they are locked.

working_the_terrain.title: Working the Terrain
working_the_terrain.description:
Face a terrain feature and press the action button to work it. Fell trees with an axe, mine rocks with a war pick, a heavy weapon or a pickaxe, pick plants by hand. Anything can be dismantled.

You get crafting materials. Mining sometimes gives an ingot.

Foraging always gives plant matter and sometimes something to eat, depending on the region. Training Foraging improves your finds.

Alien planets have nothing to forage. Food there comes from butchering wildlife.

Felled trees and worked features stay gone.

the_dungeon_and_the_tower.title: The Dungeon and the Tower
the_dungeon_and_the_tower.description:
One great dungeon, its layout rolled when the world is created.

Above ground it runs in ten levels, A to J, each of nine ordinary floors and one elevator floor. The elevator and the floor list jump to any floor already reached; unseen floors show as question marks.

Below ground is the lower tower, ninety two generated floors, each one of the structures from the procedural catalogue. Stairs read the other way down there: deeper is a smaller number.

puzzles.title: Puzzles
puzzles.description:
Maps can have puzzles:

- sokoban blocks, pits that swallow them, goal tiles, reset and undo shrines
- pressure plates, timed plates that must be held, levers, gates wired with and / or logic
- ice floors, arrow tiles, conveyors
- crystal switches that flip sets of blocks between solid and open
- torches to light, sometimes timed, sometimes spreading fire
- colour tiles, lights out grids, coloured doors, combination locks
- warp pads, crackable walls, light beams to redirect, clones that copy your moves, magnetic objects, counterweights, floodable rooms

fog_of_war.title: Fog of War
fog_of_war.description:
Some maps are covered in fog that clears as you walk. Vision is a cone: you see where you face, and turning is how you look around.

Uncovered ground is remembered per map.

digging_and_secret_doors.title: Digging and Secret Doors
digging_and_secret_doors.description:
Some walls can be broken through at runtime, turning a dead end into a route. Digging is the deliberate version.

Secret doors look like wall until interacted with, then fade, make a noise and stay open.

Locked doors give three options. Peek teleports you for a look without letting you move, and the menu that follows holds the other two: pick, which plays a falling block minigame and needs lockpicks, or break in, which is filed as a crime.

water,_climbing_and_bridges.title: Water, Climbing and Bridges
water,_climbing_and_bridges.description:
Face water and press the action button: swim (no running), fish (needs a rod), or dive.

Climbing is slow and companions hide while you climb. Jumping down from high up hurts, more the farther you fall.

Bridges have layers. Walk on from the approach to cross over it; come from anywhere else to pass under it.

A mirror shows the reflection of whoever stands in front of it.

weather,_time_and_seasons.title: Weather, Time and Seasons
weather,_time_and_seasons.description:
The clock starts at 8 AM on 1 January 2001 and never stops. Time advances as you walk and jumps when you sleep, wait or travel.

Weather is generated per country from the date, and changes on entering an outdoor map. The country sets sunrise and sunset, seasonal temperatures, and which weather is possible.

Rain applies Wet, storms apply Static, snow applies Hot, from the body burning to stay warm.

The screen is tinted by time of day and by temperature, blue for cold and red for hot. Rain and night have their own ambient sound channel.

dreams.title: Dreams
dreams.description:
Sleeping can drop you into a dream: a 3D world that mixes places like backrooms, offices, endless stairs, drowned places, cosmic voids, car parks, hospitals, cathedrals, factories, carnivals, sewers, gardens and ruins.

- WASD walks, the mouse looks, space jumps. Hold jump while standing still to take off
- the action button uses the weapon in your right hand; the wheel switches weapons
- touching anything alive takes you to another dream, and so does walking straight into a wall
- holes have no floor, and falling far enough wakes you up

Each dream has strange rules: breathing ground, odd gravity, inverted colours, figures that move only when unwatched, time skips, changing size.

Dreams never end. Time spent inside can earn knowledge, reported when you wake.

adventures_on_the_map.title: Adventures on the Map
adventures_on_the_map.description:
Some world map squares show a "???" marker, redrawn once a day. Stand on it and Investigate plays a branching adventure written for that place.

The last node pays out: a relic, gear, salvage, money, a fight with something native, a minigame, an augment, a change of faction standing, a crime filed against you, a rest, or nothing.

The leader goes in and the companion at their shoulder comments in their own register. Some choices are only offered to a leader of a particular temperament, and the prose is combinatorial.

A biome has one marker, two if it is very large, and a named place has one more. A resolved square stays resolved.

bologna.title: Bologna
bologna.description:
Bologna is in the game as itself, rasterised from OpenStreetMap into a grid of large cells that join seamlessly at the borders.

Every rasterised building has a door on its south face and every door is a way in. Most are homes; a share are shops and inns, seeded per cell and per tile, so a door is always the same business.

The cells have no hand placed events. The city is populated at runtime: townspeople drawn from the world's own faces and from Bolognesi born there, plus wildlife by habitat, street animals on pavements, waterfowl and fish in the canals, birds on rooftops.

platformer_maps.title: Platformer Maps
platformer_maps.description:
On a map tagged as a platform stage the controls become a side scroller: left and right walk, space jumps, shift runs, gravity pulls, and jumping against a wall kicks off it.

Ladders are climbed with up. Companions follow your exact path a moment behind.

flying.title: Flying
flying.description:
Flight moves you like an airship: freely, in any direction, over everything. Confirm lands you.

It comes from particular items, skills and vehicles rather than being held permanently.

the_map_of_maps.title: The Map of Maps
the_map_of_maps.description:
A second map shows every map you know and how they connect, built from the transfer events and doors between them.

Click a node to set it as destination and the shortest path lights up. A compass appears in the corner pointing at the next waypoint and goes away on arrival.

chests_and_treasure_rooms.title: Chests and Treasure Rooms
chests_and_treasure_rooms.description:
Chest contents scale with the party's median level. An emptied chest stays empty, and open chests stay open.

Some maps hide treasure rooms: reachable, randomly placed rooms with richer contents.

research_and_discovery.title: Research and Discovery
research_and_discovery.description:
Eight trees of discovery, one per discipline: Social Sciences, Alchemistry, Technomagica, Physics, Arcane, Mathematics, Astronomy, Theotecnical.

The scientific trees follow real progress from 2001 to 2012. Arcane and Technomagica follow the rediscovery of lost magic and its fusion with machinery. Theotecnical follows the Vatican rebuilding its dogma around engines. Each also has fringe branches and a few nodes generated from the world seed.

Completed nodes record the leader who got there first. Researching one consumes crafting materials and returns most of that cost as refined byproducts.

fast_travel.title: Fast Travel
fast_travel.description:
Any place marked as a destination can be travelled to instead of walked to. Bus stops and signposts open the travel screen.

A destination and a mode put you on a travel map for that transport, with a countdown that keeps running while you open menus or fight and survives scene changes. At zero you arrive.

Companions talk in transit, vehicle crews sleep in shifts, and the world clock keeps moving.

the_thirty_ways_to_travel.title: The Thirty Ways to Travel
the_thirty_ways_to_travel.description:
Each destination lists the transports that reach it. There are thirty, trading money for time.

Walking is free and slowest. A bicycle is cheap and a bit faster, a horse better still, and car sharing or the camper cost fuel instead of money.

Bus, train, taxi, boat and ferry are the ordinary fares. The train is good value; the taxi is as fast but costs more.

Flights, limousines, helicopters and private jets are expensive and fast. Cruises, submarines, balloons and zeppelins are slow and expensive.

The exotic options include magic carpets, dragons, teleport circles, hypermetro, maglev, hyperloop, starships, wormholes, quantum jumps, time machines and dimensional crossings. The fastest cost the most.

Longer trips cost more.

owning_a_vehicle.title: Owning a Vehicle
owning_a_vehicle.description:
You own a vehicle if you hold its key, deed or broom. It then appears in the Vehicles menu and can be summoned and driven.

Vehicles stay parked where you leave them. If several are on one tile, you'll be asked which one you mean.

Walk up to a parked vehicle to open its menu: drive, enter, storage, refuel, repair.

The camper, the car and the starship have interiors you can walk in, with storage.

vehicle_the_camper.title: Vehicle: The Camper
vehicle_the_camper.description:
The largest vehicle. A hundred litres of fuel, a walk in interior with beds and storage, repairable and upgradable, refuels at any roadside pump.

A ground vehicle, so it crosses road tiles faster than open country, and fast travel by camper costs fuel rather than money.

Two workshop modules extend it. Aquatic makes it float and dive, with C to dive and surface. Flight fits rotors, with F to take off and land.

Driving it opens a 3D scene, and a crew lives aboard it.

vehicle_the_car.title: Vehicle: The Car
vehicle_the_car.description:
Faster than the camper and much smaller. Sixty litres of fuel, a small interior, refuels at any pump, takes the road bonus, and fast travel by car costs fuel rather than money.

Any parked car on the map can be stolen: face it, press the action button and choose to steal. That opens the lockpicking minigame and needs a lockpick, or a skeleton key, which opens it outright. Success hands you its keys and removes the car from the world. Failure files a vehicle theft against you.

vehicle_the_bike.title: Vehicle: The Bike
vehicle_the_bike.description:
Human powered, so it needs no fuel and cannot run dry. The fastest vehicle available early, takes the road bonus, and has no interior, no storage and no repair costs.

No crew rota: the rider does everything.

vehicle_the_flying_broom.title: Vehicle: The Flying Broom
vehicle_the_flying_broom.description:
Needs no fuel, works indoors, and stows into your pack as an item.

It flies, so it passes over every tile of every map: walls, water, cliffs and events. It lands on anything that can be stood on, rooftops and bridges included, and is boarded from the tile it landed on.

It takes no road bonus.

vehicle_the_boat.title: Vehicle: The Boat
vehicle_the_boat.description:
An inflatable dinghy. No fuel, no interior, no storage, no repairs, and it travels only on open water.

The party is drawn aboard: everyone on the benches, bow first, facing the way they are going, with the pet in the stern.

vehicle_the_starship.title: Vehicle: The Starship
vehicle_the_starship.description:
Two hundred litres of fuel and a full walk in interior. It cannot be refuelled at a roadside pump.

Hull, layout and appearance are generated from a set of trait axes and can be edited.

It needs no driver and flies itself, so its crew page covers living aboard rather than driving. It is used from the star map.

fuel.title: Fuel
fuel.description:
The camper, the car and the starship burn fuel. The bike, the broom and the boat do not.

Fuel is bought at pumps at a price that moves with the world's oil market. The camper and the car fill at any roadside pump; the starship cannot.

Consumption is by distance and differs per vehicle, with a gauge in the corner while driving. Running dry strands you.

vehicle_damage_and_repair.title: Vehicle Damage and Repair
vehicle_damage_and_repair.description:
A vehicle has twelve parts, each with its own health. Engine, transmission, brakes and steering are critical and stop it dead when broken; battery, alternator, radiator, fuel system, exhaust, suspension, tyres and body only cost performance.

Damage comes from what you hit. Something soft marks the front only; another vehicle at road speed is felt throughout. The notification names the parts.

Repairs consume crafting materials, scaled by the depth of the repair. While riding, the vehicle's condition is drawn as an HP bar on the party HUD.

the_workshop.title: The Workshop
the_workshop.description:
Vehicles are upgraded with crafting materials at the workshop.

Four upgrades, three levels each: acceleration, speed, fuel capacity and structural health. Two one off modules, camper only: aquatic, which floats and dives, and flight, which fits rotors.

Aerodynamic work reduces how much game time a world map tile costs.

Each level costs more exotic materials, from steel and plastic through titanium and circuitry to varlenian matter, nanotubes and quantum components.

the_crew.title: The Crew
the_crew.description:
The leader drives when a journey starts, and only the driver earns the vehicle's specialization experience.

Driving tires people out. When the driver gets too tired, the best rested member takes over. If nobody can, the driver keeps going and you are told.

Tired passengers nap until rested or until the trip ends. They wake if the party gets out, someone enters the cabin, or there is a crash.

The bike and the broom have no rota. The starship flies itself, and its crew looks after their needs from the hold.

driving_in_3d.title: Driving in 3D
driving_in_3d.description:
Driving the camper opens a 3D road scene built from the world map: the same biomes, mountains, water, roads, cities and forests.

Three views, switched with Tab or Y: first person behind the wheel, chase camera with zoom, and a free cabin view through a door.

W accelerates, Shift is turbo, S brakes and reverses, A and D steer, space is the handbrake, the mouse looks.

Grip changes with the surface, the handbrake drifts, and slopes matter.

Traffic brakes, takes junctions and can be crashed into.

On foot the leader holds their weapon, and the d-pad switches weapons. Roadside enemies match the biome.

traffic,_roadkill_and_theft.title: Traffic, Roadkill and Theft
traffic,_roadkill_and_theft.description:
Cars drive around the maps on their own.

Only moving cars hit things. Town traffic brakes for people; highway traffic does not.

Getting hit knocks you clear and counts as an accident. NPCs hit by a car get injured; creatures hit hard enough die.

Running someone over injures them, makes them like the whole party less, and counts as a hit and run. Ramming the same creature over and over makes it likely to fight back.

Sometimes a driver pulls over and gets out for a while. Their car stays parked and can be stolen.

people_are_real_here.title: People Are Real Here
people_are_real_here.description:
Every person on the map has a full profile, generated from their name and the world seed:

- a personality out of twenty five archetypes, which sets how they speak
- traits, the same ones your characters have
- an ideology on five axes: economy, authority, tradition, militarism, mysticism
- wealth, skills, inventory and equipment
- a faction, a home, a job and a schedule
- a backstory drawn from your world's history
- a medical history, past diseases and badly healed bones included

Part of the population is animals, minted from the same system. A creature on a beast class is non sentient: no conversation, no politics, no savings, no property.

the_empathize_panel.title: The Empathize Panel
the_empathize_panel.description:
Talking to someone properly opens the Empathize panel: identity, history, biology, health, romantic life, daily life, politics, and a log of their last conversations.

From it you can talk, praise, insult, joke, give, trade, court, propose, recruit, and read why they feel as they do about you.

Standings are per party member, and only the member doing the talking moves theirs.

A free chat field takes typed input and generates a reply. With the local language model enabled it writes the reply; otherwise a Markov chain does.

how_somebody_decides_what_they_think_of_.title: How Somebody Decides What They Think of You
how_somebody_decides_what_they_think_of_.description:
An NPC's opinion of each of your characters comes from four things:

- how you have treated them
- how well your traits match
- how close your politics are
- how you both smell right now

Gaining standing also fills the Company need of whoever gained it.

Attraction is separate. Talk, gifts and trade change opinion; courting changes attraction, and traits and hygiene count extra there.

people_have_lives.title: People Have Lives
people_have_lives.description:
Everyone's life advances whenever time does: minute by minute, and through any skip.

- they are born somewhere on a date and keep a record of every move since, with reasons
- they meet, date, marry, divorce and separate, preferring partners from their own settlement
- they hold careers from the real job list, with a history from their first working year, changes as they age, and retirement
- dishonest ones have convictions, sentences served off screen and outstanding bounties, and a conviction can cost someone their job

A year spent in cryogenic sleep is a year in which everyone aged, changed jobs, married and buried each other.

what_people_say_to_each_other.title: What People Say to Each Other
what_people_say_to_each_other.description:
Two people who wander close together stop, face each other and hold a conversation, one line at a time in thought bubbles. The tone, positive, negative, neutral or a debate, comes from what they think of each other and from their personalities. Finishing one moves both opinions.

People sharing a room while busy trade two line exchanges without stopping.

Each of the twenty five personalities has its own lines for weather and time of day, its own inner monologue, and its own openers and closers.

The last twenty conversations of every person can be read in their panel.

settlements_and_what_happens_to_them.title: Settlements and What Happens To Them
settlements_and_what_happens_to_them.description:
Every settlement has three civic meters. Prosperity comes from employment, the national economy and recent events; security from crime per head, the honesty of the local captain of the guard, national stability and how wanted you are; mood from the other two plus unrest, festivals, epidemics and street traffic.

Episodes sit on top of them:

- crime wave: starts when security collapses. Crime pays better and the crackdown catches more thieves, so the wave dies down
- boom and bust: start at the extremes of prosperity and swing hiring, crime, divorce, shop prices and market sentiment, then erode their own cause
- festival: declared by a thriving town. Mood and bustle up, shops fuller, pickpockets working the crowds
- epidemic: rare, and worse in miserable towns. Mood, hiring and shop traffic collapse until it burns out

Unemployment feeds crime, crime feeds crackdowns, crackdowns feed prisons, prisons feed unemployment. All of it reaches the news, the stock market, hiring and gossip.

politics.title: Politics
politics.description:
Every hyperpower has a government, and their shapes differ: theocracies, single party states, parliamentary monarchies, technocracies, sultanates, divine pantheons, serene republics, corporatocracies, warband confederacies. Each has parties, orders or clans, a political class with charisma, integrity, cunning and ambition, a head of state, and meters for legitimacy, stability, unrest, economy and treasury.

Elections run in each power's own idiom: general elections, papal conclaves over several ballots, politburo plenums announcing 99% results, wealth weighted shareholder meetings, goblin moots where the runner up risks being eaten, divine ascension tournaments, palace successions, and the Archive's Great Examination.

Between elections: scandals, edicts, protests, riots, coups, revolutions, assassinations, referendums, and rulers ageing and dying.

Every person has a political identity: five axis ideology, a party, an engagement level from apathetic to organizer, a voting record, and grudges against the parties that beat theirs.

Each settlement elects a mayor every year, who appoints a captain of the guard, a tax collector and a high priest from among their allies.

factions_and_reputation.title: Factions and Reputation
factions_and_reputation.description:
Eighteen factions. Standing with each runs from -100 to +100, moved by contracts taken, crimes committed, adventures resolved and sides taken.

Some factions belong to a hyperpower and are a branch of it, so credit earned with the parent can extend to its branches.

Standing decides what work is offered, what prices are quoted, who will speak to you, and which seats you may take.

the_assembly.title: The Assembly
the_assembly.description:
Every hyperpower holds a seat on neutral ground inside the Omega Tower. Once a week of game time the delegations argue about alliances, trade, war and recent events.

A party member can take a seat. The seat, the standing it earns and the weekly stipend are that character's alone, and the stipend scales with their standing with the power they serve. Let it fall far enough and they are dismissed. Only powers that already think neutrally or well of them will take them, a character joins once, and resigning costs far more than joining paid.

A session rolls one to three motions. Two to five delegations take the floor, each in its own voice, you answer, and every seat votes. Votes are either public, with each named tile turning green or red, or secret, where only the total is shown.

Grave motions, war, admission, territory, artifacts, theonuclear devices and the goblin question, go to the Security Council: the five strongest powers after the century of history. Majority carries and the Secretary General breaks a tie; without one, the motion fails.

The Tourists hold a chair with no ballot, take the floor when they like, and admit nobody.

crime_and_bounty.title: Crime and Bounty
crime_and_bounty.description:
Every crime is filed by name with its own bounty value, and your bounty is the sum of them. Deliberate crimes: theft, breaking and entering, vehicle theft. Accidental ones too, such as running someone over.

Bounty lowers the security meter of settlements you are in, becomes gossip, changes how the guard behaves, and is read out in court.

The record can be viewed at any time and settled through the police portal.

the_police_portal.title: The Police Portal
the_police_portal.description:
The N€police application on the Hypernet is the continental police portal, and it settles your record without waiting for you to be caught.

- case file: every charge with its fine, settled one at a time or all at once
- self-report: confess something not yet registered, at half the usual fine
- custody: turn yourself in, or request a hearing before Eris

Both custody options leave the computer, because the cells and the courtroom are places on the map.

the_trial.title: The Trial
the_trial.description:
Justice is administered by Eris, and a trial is generated rather than scripted. The courtroom, gallery, staff and ambience are rolled fresh each time, and she cites invented case law and produces invented exhibits mid hearing.

Counsel is retained before the hearing opens: hire one of five advocates, nominate a party member, or stand alone. The five are people from your world, fixed for its lifetime, and recruiting one strikes them off the bar.

The brief shows each option's level, INT, WIS, Law level, opinion of you, fee, and the projected odds of every outcome, computed with the model the verdict runs on. The odds swing on Eris's mood, and in some moods she throws counsel out: you lose their bonus and the fee is not refunded.

Defending yourself, or having a companion defend you, earns a few points of the Law specialization per hearing, which improves the odds. A professional teaches the party nothing.

The hearing is a plea, then a series of choices, then a verdict that depends heavily on her mood. Evenings spent with Eris raise a bond, and a defendant she has dined with meets a warmer mood wheel, a lower conviction chance and shorter sentences.

Sandbox mode has a reverse trial, where you play Eris.

sentences_and_prison.title: Sentences and Prison
sentences_and_prison.description:
Sentences come in two shapes. A named term is served by the game clock: time passes in the cells and the bounty is cleared on release. An open ended sentence has no release date and grinds the bounty down day by day.

Turning yourself in at the police portal goes straight to the second kind without a hearing.

On release, Eris comments based on your relationship.

dating_eris.title: Dating Eris
dating_eris.description:
Eris can be courted, and an evening with her is a generated scene.

It happens in a biome, and each biome owns its opening, its questions, its romantic beat, its chaotic beat, its shared activity and its local incidents. A scenario is rolled on top, picnic, seance, stakeout and others, so one biome hosts many evenings.

Her mood is rolled from sixteen: playful, romantic, chaotic, nervous, confident, caring, guilty, crazed, psyched out, high on solipsism, eldritch, melancholy, smug, paranoid, prophetic, bored. It can shift mid date. In the eldritch mood her lines warp, her pulse reads things that are not numbers, and the portrait misbehaves.

Each date also rolls a register, sincere, capricious or completely bonkers, which scales how often the evening is interrupted and how hard her feelings swing. She interrupts with dares, up to robbing a bank. Your own answers are generated too, and how she takes one is a roll of her mood.

Two heartbeats are drawn on screen, yours and hers. She remembers past dates, keeps a separate score for every party member, and sometimes turns towards one of your companions mid date.

The first date that ends well pays an expression seed, once per save.

the_post.title: The Post
the_post.description:
You can write to another party in the same world, or in a different world on your computer. The letter waits until someone plays that party.

You can set a delivery date days, months or years ahead. A delayed letter to your own party is a letter to your future self.

Money and goods can be enclosed. They leave your pockets at once and arrive when the letter is collected.

Post inside one world is free. Sending to another world is very expensive, and the price follows oil and soul prices.

the_news.title: The News
the_news.description:
The world writes its own news, and news items have effects: property prices, shop occupancy, market sentiment.

Settlement episodes, riots, coups, elections, epidemics and the mayor's divorce all become headlines. The real estate market moves on them, the stock market takes sentiment from them, and people talk about them.

the_party_diary.title: The Party Diary
the_party_diary.description:
The diary is the record one party keeps of its own life, written as it happens.

It takes in journeys and arrivals, landings and warps, first entry into a named place, dungeon floors, sleeping and waiting, cryogenic sleep, fights won and lost, bosses, arena streaks, people joining and leaving, deaths, levels, pets, creatures talked round, births, friendships, enmities, courtships, evenings with Eris, diseases, limbs lost, augments, surgery, notable finds, purchases and sales, thefts, property, loans, share trades, crimes, trials, prison, shifts worked, crops, forging, cooking, brewing, building, skills, research, quests, bestiary entries, minigames, television and dreams.

Not recorded: ordinary conversation, statue descriptions, states coming and going, discarded items.

Entries are stored as keys, so a diary written in one language reads correctly in another. The banter system takes the newest lines and turns them into what the party talks about.

conversation_topics.title: Conversation Topics
conversation_topics.description:
Some dialogue teaches a topic, written in square brackets in the line where it appears. Once one character hears it, the whole party knows it.

A dialogue option that requires a topic stays hidden until you know it, rather than greyed out.

Every topic learned is announced. The Topics tab of this book lists them with who knows each one, and some have a page of their own.

armies.title: Armies
armies.description:
Beyond the party of three there is an army. Troops are recruited by faction, up to a hundred, and the count is drawn over your sprite on the world map.

Other armies fill the world map. About a fifth are faction armies of two hundred to a thousand troops, which stay inside their own country's borders. The rest are independent bands of five to thirty, which roam anywhere and spawn near you.

Touching one starts a field battle in a real time tactical view: your units in yellow, theirs in red, formed up by role, close quarters in front, support behind, ranged at the back, fighting on their own stats. Wounded troops drop to one hit point and stop; killed troops are gone for good.

multiplayer.title: Multiplayer
multiplayer.description:
Two ways to play with other people.

Online, through a central server or through Steam. A server session supports many players, of whom the nearest eight are drawn on one map. A Steam lobby caps at eight and sets rich presence, so friends see Join Game in their list.

Local split screen, two players on one machine with a gamepad each. The viewports are independent and merge into one when the players are close, and player two interacts with events directly.

Split screen also runs a hot seat for minigames without a split screen session on the overworld. Real time arcade carts let either player steer; chess, pool and bowling alternate turns.

During a map battle the viewports merge and player two drives the second party member.

the_century_behind_you.title: The Century Behind You
the_century_behind_you.description:
Before you take a step, the world has lived through a century: a generated alternate history of Europe from 1900 to 2001.

It produces coups, elections, purges and assassinations; wars, sieges, mutinies and conquests; fifty kinds of paranormal anomaly, occult rites and the Squishing itself; scientific expeditions, natural disasters and organised crime; economic shifts and technological breakthroughs. The weighting favours the paranormal and the occult.

That history sets which hyperpowers exist and how strong they are, which five sit on the Security Council, what epidemics the last century saw, and what the people you meet lived through.

The full timeline is readable in the Historical Archive.

money.title: Money
money.description:
Money is euros, written with two decimal places.

There is no other currency except at the arcade, where euros buy tokens and tokens sell back at a fixed rate.

The Assets screen adds cash, bank balance, property, shares and livestock, subtracts debts, and calls the result net worth.

shops.title: Shops
shops.description:
There are several kinds of shop.

- counter shop: goods by category, sorted by price, with a detail card
- delivery order: arrives in a few days, cheaper items sooner
- random daily shop: different stock every day
- vending machine: a grid of coded products, with a daily limit per slot
- teaching shop: sells skills instead of goods, at a discount

Everything except skills is taxed, and the rate follows the economy. Empty shops restock at midnight.

stealing.title: Stealing
stealing.description:
Anything on a shop's shelves can be stolen. The steal window lists what nearby shops hold, with your chance for each item. Agility helps; heavy and valuable items are harder.

Daily merchants can only be robbed from close by.

Getting caught is a crime and makes the town less safe. During a crime wave, stealing is harder.

banking_and_loans.title: Banking and Loans
banking_and_loans.description:
The bank takes deposits, pays interest on the balance, and lends at interest against a due date. Both run on the world clock, so they accrue while you walk, sleep, travel or sit in cryogenic sleep.

Missing the due date is penalised. The Assets screen shows the balance, the outstanding loan and the date.

the_stock_market.title: The Stock Market
the_stock_market.description:
The market trades two commodities, oil and soul crystals, from a single page terminal. Prices move at random, pushed by what happens in the world: settlement booms and busts, news events, the state of the powers.

The Assets screen draws the live graph over your portfolio. The oil price is also what the fuel pump charges and what a letter to another dimension costs.

real_estate.title: Real Estate
real_estate.description:
Properties across the towns are rated one to five stars. Cheap ones are affordable; four and five stars are estates.

Buy one and you can rent it to NPCs for regular income. Rent one yourself and you pay monthly, with no subletting; miss payments and you are evicted.

Prices move with local news.

Inn rooms are separate: one booking covers a full day.

owning_a_shop.title: Owning a Shop
owning_a_shop.description:
A shop you own holds stock, a warehouse and a production line. Items with recipes can be produced from materials on the premises, deliveries are made at delivery points on the maps, and NPC staff can be hired to do the work.

Four pages: overview, shelf stock, warehouse, and the catalogue of what can be produced.

work.title: Work
work.description:
More than thirty jobs across several categories, and any party member can be sent to work.

Each job states its stat requirements first, and a member short of them is flagged but never blocked.

A shift takes game time, the screen darkens, and the outcome is generated from the worker's stats and luck. Pay is money; a disaster can cost money, deal damage, or leave a status effect.

The Job Offers menu lists what is available now and where.

quests.title: Quests
quests.description:
Quests are generated, and each board offers jobs that suit where it stands.

A quest has one or more steps:

- reach a place on the world map
- open a hidden chest, or dig a site (needs a shovel)
- land on a planet and open its sample cache
- kill a specific strong enemy
- scan statues or signposts, or clear trees, rocks or rubble
- visit another town's board, or interview someone through Empathize
- hand over items, or wait for a delivery
- win arena fights, defeat enemies, or hold oil shares

Terms are shown before you accept: reward, cost, deadline, penalties and reputation. Scams lie about them.

Rewards and difficulty follow your party's level. The board's second tab tracks your contracts, where you collect or abandon them.

The quest log is a board of sticky notes in three columns that you can drag between.

reading_a_notice.title: Reading a Notice
reading_a_notice.description:
A quest notice is written in the voice of whoever pinned it up. Dozens of faction registers and a couple of dozen personality registers exist: a corporate contract, a goblin scrawl, a redacted military bill, a nervous private plea.

What is left out, what is over explained and what is plainly a lie are readable before you accept. The terms panel gives the numbers.

arcade_tokens.title: Arcade Tokens
arcade_tokens.description:
